summary: Describes the end-to-end protocol, block formats, and abstract service for exchanging bundles of messages in Delay Tolerant Networking. It came from the IRTF DTN Research Group and is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: The Bundle Protocol moves data through networks where connections may be unavailable for long periods. Each node can store a bundle and forward it when a suitable connection is available.

questions: what is custody transfer in dtn
subtitle: A store-and-forward protocol for exchanging bundles across networks with intermittent connectivity.

tldr.problem: Some networks have intermittent connectivity, long or variable delays, and high bit error rates, making continuous end-to-end communication difficult.
tldr.mechanism: The Bundle Protocol carries blocks of data between nodes in bundles, which can be stored, forwarded, fragmented, and tracked with custody signals.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5050 specifies version 6 of an Experimental protocol and is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

sections.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking
sections.content:
RFC 5050 describes version 6 of the Bundle Protocol (BP) for Delay-Tolerant Networking. BP operates at the application layer as a store-and-forward overlay across networks that may have intermittent connectivity, large or variable delays, or high bit error rates.

Bundle nodes use convergence layer adapters to carry bundles over their local network protocols. This RFC defines bundle formats and abstract services, but not routing algorithms or how forwarding tables are populated.
sections.plainLanguage: BP carries application data across networks that may not have a continuous connection. Nodes store bundles and pass them along using the network available to them.

sections.title: Nodes, Endpoints, and Delivery
sections.content:
A bundle node includes a Bundle Protocol Agent, convergence layer adapters, and an Application Agent. The Bundle Protocol Agent runs the protocol, adapters communicate over local networks, and application agents request transmission or receive delivered data.

An endpoint is a set of nodes identified by an endpoint ID. An application registers a node with an endpoint as Active or Passive. Active registrations receive deliverable bundles automatically; Passive registrations can defer delivery until polled or abandon it according to their configured action.
sections.plainLanguage: Nodes use endpoint IDs to name destinations. Applications can receive bundles automatically or wait and request them later.

sections.title: Bundle Blocks and Numeric Values
sections.content:
A bundle consists of at least two blocks. The first is the primary block, which contains routing information, endpoint references, a creation timestamp, a lifetime, and a dictionary. At most one block is the payload block; additional extension blocks may support other functions.

Most numeric fields use a Self-Delimiting Numeric Value (SDNV), which carries 7 value bits in each octet and marks whether more octets follow. Endpoint IDs are URIs with a scheme name and scheme-specific part; the primary block's dictionary can store their text once and refer to it by offsets.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle starts with a primary block that identifies its endpoints and timing, followed by its payload and optional extension blocks. Compact numeric fields and a shared dictionary reduce repeated data.

sections.title: Forwarding, Fragmentation, and Custody
sections.content:
A node may forward a bundle directly to its destination or to another endpoint for later forwarding. Bundles expire when their lifetime ends. If a contact is too short for a whole bundle, a node may fragment it unless its flags prohibit fragmentation; the destination reassembles the payload from fragments.

With custody transfer, a node that accepts custody commits to retaining a copy until custody is released. It can send custody signals to the previous custodian. Status reports can record reception, custody acceptance, forwarding, delivery, or deletion.
sections.plainLanguage: Nodes forward bundles when a route is available and may split them when a contact cannot carry the whole bundle. A custodian keeps a copy until another node takes responsibility or delivery is confirmed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC expects bundle security services to be specified in the accompanying Bundle Security Protocol. Security concerns include preventing unauthorized use of scarce network resources, protecting payload integrity across long delays, and providing confidentiality when needed.

Three security blocks provide different services: the Bundle Authentication Block supports hop-by-hop authenticity and integrity; the Payload Security Block supports security-source to security-destination authenticity and integrity; and the Confidentiality Block identifies the algorithm and key IDs used to encrypt the payload. Forwarding nodes must preserve block order so they do not invalidate security.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate security blocks can authenticate bundles, protect integrity, or encrypt payloads. Forwarding nodes must preserve bundle structure so those protections continue to work.
